findings.label: Small/medium timing workloads are host-launch bound: device kernel is 2.69 us against 62.75 us eval latency
findings.backend_detail: msprof op_summary per-invocation rows; 110 kernel invocations of _round_flat, task_type AI_VECTOR_CORE

evidence.metric: min/max task duration spread across 110 invocations

findings.inference: The eval latency for this workload is 62.753 us (authoritative, from get_profile_context) while the msprof device kernel duration is 2.694 us. Device is therefore only 4.3% of the measured call; about 60 us is host-side. This is not explained by undersized work inside the kernel: Block Num=1 and aiv_total_cycles=3566.48 over aiv_time_us=2.1615 gives ~1.65 GHz of single-core cycles, i.e. exactly the one-program grid that ceil(1024/4096) produces, so the 2.7 us figure is genuine single-AIV work and not a truncated launch. The ~63 us floor is flat across timing-0 (1024 elem), timing-9 (65536) and timing-10 (1048576), a 1024x element range whose device time must differ by roughly an order of magnitude, so the floor cannot be device work; it is a fixed per-call host cost in the candidate's `_dispatch` + Triton launch path. The eval reference (torch.round) completes the same case in 14.247 us including its own launch, which bounds total harness overhead at about 14 us and leaves ~48 us attributable to the candidate's own Python launch path.

findings.label: Large 4096x4096 cases are vector-instruction bound, not bandwidth bound; fp16 and fp32 take near-identical time at 2x byte difference
findings.backend_detail: msprof aiv_* pipeline counters, AI_VECTOR_CORE; 100-110 invocations averaged
findings.inference: All three large workloads process the identical element count (4096x4096 = 16,777,216). fp16 moves 67.1 MB (2 bytes read + 2 bytes written) and takes 176.13 us => 381 GB/s logical; fp32 moves 134.2 MB and takes 185.66 us => 723 GB/s logical. Doubling the bytes moved costs only +5.4% time, and the fp32 MTE2 ratio is 1.72x the fp16 one while the duration is essentially unchanged. If the kernel were memory bound the fp32 case would be roughly twice the fp16 time. Instead the vector pipe ratio (0.675 fp16 / 0.678 bf16 / 0.583 fp32) dominates and the MTE ratios stay at 0.09-0.20. Time therefore scales with elements/vector-ops, not with bytes. Calibrated arithmetic for the per-element instruction count: aiv_total_cycles 11,517,310 over aiv_time_us 175.53 gives 65.6 GHz aggregate; divided across 40 AIV subcores gives ~1.64 GHz per core, so aiv_vec_time_us 118.47 corresponds to ~194,300 vector-issue cycles per core for 16,777,216/40 = 419,430 elements = 6,554 vector groups of 64 fp32 lanes, i.e. ~29.6 issue cycles per 64-element group. The source `_rnd_value` emits roughly 12-14 fp32 vector ops per element (convert in, mul, abs-mask, add, sub, compare, select, bitcast-or, optional reciprocal mul, select for NaN/Inf, convert out); at ~2 cycles per vector issue that accounts for 24-28 of the 29.6 cycles. The fp32-emulation arithmetic itself, not the memory system, sets the large-case duration. Note the ratios overlap (vec+mte2+mte3+mte1 exceed 1) so they must not be summed into a time decomposition, and MTE activity ratio is not HBM peak utilization. I did not obtain the instruction listing, so the per-op count above is arithmetic inference from counters plus source, not a measured SASS/instruction histogram.

findings.label: Masked load/store path is executed for every program even where the grid exactly divides N; scalar pipe is 15-16% of large-case device time
findings.backend_detail: msprof op_summary Block Num and aiv_scalar_* counters; source lines 35-39 of the evaluated candidate
findings.inference: For all three large workloads N = 4096*4096 = 16,777,216 and the observed Block Num is exactly 4096 = N/4096, so the `index < N` predicate at main.py:36 is provably all-true for every program, yet the kernel is compiled and executed with the predicate and the `tl.load(..., mask=..., other=0.0)` zero-fill path on both the load (line 37) and the store (line 39). The scalar pipe is busy 28.75 us of 175.53 us (16.4%) on the fp16 case and 15.1% on fp32, which is consistent with per-element integer index/compare/select address arithmetic and predicate maintenance rather than with a bandwidth stall. icache miss rate is 0 so the scalar time is not instruction fetch. I could not confirm how many predicated instructions the backend actually emits because the instruction-level request was cancelled, so the size of the removable predicate cost is unquantified; the existence of the masked datapath and the exact-divisibility fact are measured, the cost attribution is not.

performance_interpretation: The round splits into two disjoint regimes and no single fix addresses both. (1) Nine of the twelve timing workloads (timing-0,1,2,4,5,6,8,9,10 - all 1024/65536/1048576 element cases) sit on a flat ~63-70 us floor that is indistinguishable across a 1024x range of element counts; timing-0's device kernel is only 2.694 us of its 62.753 us eval latency, so roughly 95% of the measured call is host-side launch work and only its elimination can move these workloads. Their current speedups (0.212-0.239) are limited by the candidate's own Python/Triton launch path, not by the GPU work. (2) The three 4096x4096 workloads (timing-3, timing-7, timing-11) are device bound - 176.1/179.0/185.7 us device against 173.0/172.8/180.4 us eval - and there the vector pipe is the limiter at 0.58-0.68 ratio while MTE2/MTE3 stay at 0.09-0.20. The decisive control is fp16 vs fp32 at identical element count: 2x the bytes costs +5.4% duration, so these cases are bound by the ~12-14 fp32 vector ops per element used to emulate round-half-to-even, not by traffic. The frozen baseline hypothesis (a plain masked BLOCK=4096 kernel would reveal which workloads are host-launch bound versus bandwidth bound) is supported on the first half and contradicted on the second: nothing here is bandwidth bound. Because 9 of 12 workloads are in the launch-bound regime, a host-path fix carries a 9/12 exponent into geo_mean while a 2x device kernel gain carries only 3/12.

next_experiment.action_description: Replace the per-call high-level Triton launch in `_dispatch` (main.py:76 and :78-81) with a cached compiled-artifact low-level launch: compile once per (element dtype, DECIMALS constexpr, BLOCK, contiguous-vs-strided) key, cache the compiled artifact and its packed metadata, then on every call pass the current input pointer, current output pointer, current N and the current runtime scalars (SCALE, INV_SCALE) plus the current stream into the low-level launch entry (as done in operators/campaigns/next25-20261029-v2/proposals/xlogy_scalar_tensor/runtime-scalar-v3/main.py via compiled.run.launch). Keep the existing masked kernel body, the strided kernel and the NaN/Inf/sign-bit logic unchanged; do not cache shape-dependent tensors, do not cache the runtime scalars inside a closure, and do not specialise on the nine benchmark shapes.
next_experiment.expected_impact: The nine small/medium timing workloads currently spend ~48 us of a ~63 us call above the reference's own total. Cutting that to ~10 us moves e.g. timing-0 from 62.75 us to ~15 us (speedup 0.227 -> ~0.9) and timing-1/5/9 from ~65-70 us to ~22 us (0.215-0.233 -> ~0.7). Expected geo_mean gain is the 9/12-weighted product: roughly 0.2305 -> 0.45-0.55, i.e. about +2.0x to +2.4x on the headline metric, assuming the three large workloads are unchanged. This dwarfs any device-side change: halving the large-case device time would give only 0.2305 -> ~0.27.
next_experiment.risks_and_rollback: Risks: (a) the low-level launch entry may require exact positional constexpr placeholders and can raise TypeError or silently bind stale arguments - this bit the xlogy candidate, which passed 30/30 but scored 63/72 once the runtime scalar changed; (b) a cached closure that captures the first call's decimals/scale would corrupt later calls, and `decimals` is a constexpr so a changed value must select a different cached binary, not reuse the old one; (c) the strided path takes SHAPE/XS/YS as constexpr tuples, so its cache key must include the actual shape and stride tuples and must not collide with the contiguous entry; (d) if the low-level entry bypasses the profiling/debug flags the harness relies on, preflight or profiling may break. Rollback: keep the current `Kernel[grid](...)` call intact behind a fallback branch keyed on whether the compiled artifact was obtained successfully, so reverting is a one-line switch to the pre-round launch path and the round-1 solution_sha256 remains reproducible.
success_criteria: Full formal KGS evaluation remains 30/30 PASSED and eval_status is PASSED (correctness cases 0-17 unchanged from round 1, including the two cases that reported small non-zero abs_err: correctness-15 and correctness-17).
Headline geo_mean >= 0.45 (target 0.50+), up from 0.2305, with all twelve timing workloads still PASSED.
Each of timing-0, timing-1, timing-2, timing-4, timing-5, timing-6, timing-8, timing-9, timing-10 measures below 30 us (round 1: 62.8-70.0 us).
The three large workloads timing-3, timing-7, timing-11 stay within 5% of their round-1 latencies (0.1730 / 0.1728 / 0.1804 ms), proving the change did not add device work.

Supplementary layout checks pass on the cached launch path: strided in/out with odd length, broadcast/7x9 shapes, decimals=1 versus decimals=0 back-to-back in the same process (guards the stale-constexpr and stale-scalar failure modes), non-contiguous input with the same shape as a prior contiguous call, and repeated calls with identical shape but different pointers.
Device time under msprof for timing-0 stays at or below ~3 us, confirming the eval-latency gain came from the host path and not from a changed kernel.

open_questions: Which specific component of the ~48 us excess host time dominates: Triton's Python launch/dispatch machinery, the four runtime scalar arguments, or the per-call shape/dtype/contiguity checks in `_dispatch`? A host-side timing split was not available in this round.

How many vector instructions per element does the backend actually emit for `_rnd_value`, and how many of them are predicated because of the `index < N` mask? Answering this needs the instruction listing that was cancelled.

Would an unmasked fast path, taken only when the grid provably divides N (the case for all three 4096x4096 workloads), measurably reduce the 28.7 us of scalar-pipe time, or is that scalar time mostly unavoidable index arithmetic?

Could an fp16/bf16-native rounding path (avoiding the fp32 convert) reduce large-case vector time, given that the fp32 workload shows lower vec time (107.9 us) than the fp16 one (118.5 us) at identical element count?
